transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-06-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood Obs), Priya (Orion), Marco (Orion SRE), Anna (Orion DE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focused on integrating OpenTelemetry (OTLP) token-level metrics and traces into Orion's Grafana/Tempo stack, plus runtime considerations for KV cache and batching on Redwood Dedicated/private deployments. Action items and a follow-up benchmark planned.

Topics:
- OTLP span design for LLM requests (decode, kv lookup, model infer)
- Token-level counters and histograms (per-token latency, cache hits)
- Exporter & sampling strategy (OTLP gRPC -> Tempo/Prometheus)
- Dashboard templates (Grafana) and token-explorer views
- Performance impact of tracing on batching and KV cache
- VPC/on-prem constraints and firewall/port requirements
- Quantization memory metrics and instrumentation

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ethan from Redwood. Sofia and Liam from our side, and I see Priya, Marco and Anna on the Orion side, great. 
[00:18] Priya: Hey - thanks. Today we're mainly trying to see how we can get better observability at token granularity for our product, and make sure tracing doesn't blow up latency or cost.
[00:30] Sofia: Totally. We prepared a proposed OTLP schema and some Grafana panels, we'll walk through those and then talk about runtime tradeoffs.
[00:48] Marco: quick note - our infra is VPC only, private control plane. We need to know port ranges and whether tracing needs internet egress.
[01:05] Liam: Right, we'll cover that. Short answer: you can export OTLP over private peering. For Dedicated we support OTLP gRPC to a customer collector inside the VPC, or push to Tempo/OTel collector behind the peering.
[01:30] Anna: Are there any default sampling profiles? We don't want to trace every single token for prod.
[01:40] Sofia: Good question. We recommend a mixed sampling approach: 100% of request-level spans but sampled token-level detail for 1-5% of requests, plus deterministic sampling for errors and slow p95/p99 paths.
[02:02] Priya: Can you show the span model? Conceptually what are the spans we should expect?
[02:10] Sofia: Sure, slide deck link here: https://rwd-internal.s3/gdrive/otlp-token-schema.pdf (shared). Proposed spans: 
- request.root (attributes: request_id, user_id, route, model.name, model.version)
- decode_span (tokenization)
- kv_lookup_span (attributes: kv_keys_count, kv_hit_count)
- model_inference_span (attributes: seq_len, batch_size, quant_profile)
- emit/stream_span (streaming tokens)
[03:00] Marco: How do we instrument token-level metrics? Do you recommend counters per token? That sounds heavy.
[03:10] Liam: We expose aggregated token-level metrics rather than per-token counters. Key metrics we recommend: tokens_generated_total, tokens_cached_total, kv_hits_total, kv_misses_total, token_latency_histogram (per-token latency ms), and batch_size_histogram. Those are Prometheus-style metrics exported from the runtime and also attached as span attributes for sampled traces.
[03:45] Priya: So token_latency_histogram — what's the bucket setup you use?
[03:50] Sofia: Typical buckets: 0.1ms, 0.5ms, 1ms, 2ms, 5ms, 10ms, 25ms. For per-token latency we care about p50/p95/p99, and we calculate per-request aggregates like avg_token_latency_ms.
[04:15] Anna: Any naming conventions for metrics? We want to map to our existing dashboards.
[04:20] Liam: We prefix with redwood_ so: redwood_tokens_generated_total, redwood_kv_hit_total, redwood_token_latency_ms_bucket, redwood_batch_size. Also labels: model_name, model_version, route, deployment_env, tenant_id.
[04:45] Marco: Does adding these metrics add overhead to latencies? We worry about instrumentation overhead in tight p50 budgets.
[04:55] Sofia: Minimal for counters; histograms are slightly more expensive. The bigger overhead is tracing if you capture token-level spans for every request. That's why we suggested sampling: keep full request spans always, capture token-level details for a small fraction, and attach aggregated metrics for all requests.
[05:20] Priya: How are KV cache hits exposed? We use a custom in-memory cache for prefixes.
[05:26] Ethan: Redwood runtime surfaces kv_cache_hits and kv_cache_misses as counters and exposes kv_cache_hit_rate as a derived gauge. In traces, the kv_lookup_span will include keys_queried and keys_returned attributes — note sometimes speech-to-text shows K-V cash in transcripts ;)
[05:45] Marco: Haha. Good to know. For our own collector, we currently run an OTel collector in the VPC that forwards to a central tempo+prometheus in our analytics account.
[06:00] Sofia: Perfect. Setup we recommend: Redwood -> OTel collector (gRPC) inside VPC -> local Prometheus + Tempo -> Grafana. We will provide an OTLP receiver config snippet.
[06:30] Anna: What about streaming? We need token streaming in the UI and would like to trace emit span per token chunk. Is that feasible?
[06:40] Liam: Yes, but be careful. Emitting a span per token chunk creates massive cardinality and pressure on tracing storage. Better approach: have emit_span per response with attributes about number_of_streamed_tokens and first_token_latency_ms and last_token_latency_ms. If you need to debug per-token behavior, run sampled traces that include token-level events.
[07:10] Priya: Can you walk through an example trace?
[07:15] Sofia: Example sequence: request.root -> decode_span (15ms) -> kv_lookup_span (2ms, hit=3) -> batch_enqueue_span (5ms) -> model_inference_span (120ms) -> emit_span (stream 1..n). We'll attach attributes like seq_len=2048, batch_size=8, kv_hit_rate=0.75. 
[07:50] Marco: For the model_inference_span we want to measure GPU time vs CPU orchestration. Can you split those?
[07:58] Liam: We emit separate child spans: inference.host_prep_span (CPU prep), inference.gpu_exec_span (actual kernel time), inference.kv_fill_span if applicable. GPU kernel time requires precise instrumentation in the runtime; we can surface that as an attribute inference_gpu_ms.
[08:25] Anna: Quantization — what metrics do you provide to know memory footprint and slowdown tradeoffs?
[08:30] Sofia: Redwood exposes quantization_profile labels and metrics: model_memory_bytes, active_kv_cache_bytes, model_peak_rss_bytes, and quantization_approx_error_estimate (measured from eval run). We also provide recommended quant packs (e.g., q4_0, q8_1) with expected throughput/latency deltas.
[09:00] Priya: Any examples of dashboard panels?
[09:05] Liam: We'll send a Grafana JSON but high-level panels include: token throughput (tokens/s) by route, token latency heatmap, kv_cache_hit_rate over time, batch_size distribution, model inference p50/p95/p99, trace sampling rate, and a token-explorer that lets you select a sampled trace and view per-token timestamps.
[09:35] Marco: About batching — how do you measure batched vs single-request latency?
[09:40] Sofia: Key metrics: batch_size_histogram, batch_wait_time_ms (time a request sits in queue waiting for a batch), batch_serve_time_ms (processing time for batch). Then you can compute effective per-request latency = batch_wait_time + (batch_serve_time / batch_size). We provide these as both Prom metrics and span attributes on sampled traces.
[10:10] Priya: When you run a benchmark with token-level traces on Redwood Dedicated, what should we expect in terms of overhead?
[10:18] Liam: If you only export aggregated metrics, overhead is <2-3%. If you enable token-level spans at 100% sampling, overhead can be 10-30% depending on throughput and collector backpressure. That's why realistic benchmarks sample token detail.
[10:40] Anna: For on-prem deployments, are there any special instructions for the collector?
[10:46] Sofia: On-prem we recommend colocating OTel collector with the runtime host to avoid cross-host traffic. Use the file exporter locally for heavy debug traces, or push to internal Kafka/observability pipeline. Avoid public endpoints. We'll provide a checklist.
[11:10] Marco: Firewall question — do you open specific ports for tracing or do you tunnel?
[11:16] Ethan: The preferred is to run collector inside the VPC and keep everything internal. If you must use remote exporters, you need to allow outbound gRPC to your collector endpoint on whichever port you configure (default 4317 for OTLP gRPC). If using Jaeger/HTTP you might use 14268/14250 etc. We'll include explicit port list in the checklist.
[11:45] Priya: Also security: will token data be part of traces or metrics? We need to make sure PII/token text isn't exported.
[11:55] Sofia: Redwood supports PII redaction and configurable span scrubbing. By default we do not export raw token text; token-level metrics are numeric aggregates only. Sampled traces can be configured to scrub user content. That's in the security doc we'll share.
[12:25] Marco: Can we do correlation between logs, metrics and traces? We run Loki for logs.
[12:30] Liam: Yes — ensure you forward the same trace_id across logs, metrics and traces. We add a trace_id attribute to request.root and logs can include it. Grafana can tie panels via trace_id to Tempo and Loki.
[12:50] Anna: One more practical: we'd like a 'token explorer' UI to find cold starts where kv cache miss rates spike. Does Redwood provide any tooling?
[12:58] Sofia: We ship dashboard templates that include a token-explorer like panel — it's essentially a Grafana table + drilldown to sampled trace. It surfaces request_id, kv_hit_rate, batch_size, avg_token_latency and a link to trace. We'll give you the JSON.
[13:20] Priya: Ok good. Let's discuss the benchmark plan.
[13:24] Marco: We'll run a mixed workload: 70% short chat (seq_len 128), 20% medium seq 512, 10% long seq 2048, with a mix of deterministic and streaming outputs. We want token-level metrics and 2% trace sampling.
[13:45] Ethan: Sounds good. For Dedicated run we'll allocate a 4-GPU pool and pin the model version. Redwood will provide the benchmark harness and a script to toggle sampling rates and quant profiles.
[14:05] Anna: On quant profiles, can we test q4_0 vs q8_1 and see mem + perf delta?
[14:12] Liam: Yes, we'll include recommended quant packs and expected delta table. We'll also emit quantization_profile attribute on all model_inference_spans for easy filtering.
[14:35] Priya: Anything else we should be aware of?
[14:40] Sofia: One caveat: high-cardinality labels on Prometheus (like per-user tenant_id) can blow up TSDB. Use label joins or reduce label cardinality by bucketing tenant tiers rather than raw tenant_id in metrics. Traces can carry full metadata but you should still be mindful.
[15:05] Marco: Great. Recap of next steps?
[15:09] Ethan: We'll share the OTLP config, Grafana JSON, and the security checklist. Marco will schedule benchmark and provide access. Sofia and Liam handle dashboard and quant profiles.
[15:20] Priya: Thanks, this was very practical.
[15:24] Ethan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in CRM and drop the artifacts.
